slides.label: Title
slides.notes: Welcome. This is Learning Outcome 1 of five in Basic Navigation. Confirm everyone has a 1:25 000 OS map extract and a compass in front of them, even though LO1 barely uses the compass. Say up front that the aim of LO1 is to be able to find your position on a map using nothing but what you can see on the ground.
slides.html:
2434 (Church Fenton) Squadron · Air Training Corps
Basic Navigation Using
Map and Compass
Learning Outcome 1
Finding a position on an Ordnance Survey map using the physical features of the land

slides.label: Introduction
slides.notes: Land the definition first: navigation is three questions - where am I, where am I going, what is the best way there. Then press the second point hard. Cadets on expedition habitually switch off and follow the person in front. Ask the room: if the leader dropped out right now, could you say where you are to within a hundred metres? That discomfort is the point of the lesson.
slides.html:
Introduction
What navigation actually is
Knowing where you are, where you want to go, and choosing the best route between the two.
It is map reading and compass work together — neither skill is much use on its own.
Never leave it to someone else
On expedition, check your own position and route even when you are not the one leading.
Aim to know exactly where you are on the map at any moment.

slides.label: Why map & compass
slides.notes: Do not set this up as map versus GPS - cadets rightly point out that GPS is excellent. The argument is that the electronics are a layer on top of the skill, not a replacement for it. Ask for real examples: phones dying in the cold on a winter exercise, a unit losing signal in a valley, a handset dropped in a stream. Three failure modes, all of them mundane.
slides.html:
Introduction
Why map and compass, still
GPS and phone apps are genuinely useful — but the basic knowledge is what lets you use them well, and what carries you when they stop working.
01
Batteries fail
Cold weather flattens them faster than you expect.
02
Kit gets damaged
Dropped, soaked, cracked screen — and it is gone.
03
Signal is lost
Valleys, forest and cloud all get in the way.

slides.label: LO1 statement
slides.notes: Read the outcome out loud, word for word - this is the wording cadets are assessed against. Emphasise physical features of the land: no grid references yet, no compass bearings. The whole outcome is about matching what you can see to what is printed on the map.
slides.html:
Learning Outcome 1
Be able to find a position with an Ordnance Survey map using the physical features of the land

slides.label: Section: Setting the map
slides.notes: Signpost the first half of the lesson. Two skills in this section: setting the map to the ground, and then using it to confirm exactly where you are standing. Tell them the second one is the assessed skill and the first is how you get there.
slides.html:
Part One
Setting the map
Turning the map so the ground and the paper agree — and then pinning down where you stand.

slides.label: Setting or orientating
slides.notes: The core idea: relate what is on the paper to what is in front of you, then turn the paper until they line up. Give the easy version first - following a path or a river, just rotate the map until that line matches the direction of travel. Then the payoff: junctions, bends and new features arrive where you expect them, which confirms your position as you walk. Warn them walking with the map set feels awkward at first because the writing ends up sideways or upside down. That is normal and correct.
slides.html:
Setting the map
Make the paper agree with the ground
Turn the map until identifiable features on the ground sit in their correct position relative to the paper.
THE EASY START
Following a path or river? Simply turn the map until that line runs the same way you are walking.
Now changes of direction, junctions and new features appear exactly where the map says they should — each one confirms your position.
It takes getting used to — the writing will end up sideways. Let it.
Using a high vantage point to set the map to match features on the ground.

slides.label: What features?
slides.notes: Hand this one to the cadets. Do not answer it. Give them ninety seconds in pairs on the picture, then take answers round the room. Expect: the river and its bends, the field boundaries and walls, the track, the woodland edge, the shape of the hill and the col. Push for the ones that are reliable versus the ones that change - a wall is dependable, a patch of crop is not.
slides.html:
Setting the map · exercise
What features can you use here?
Ninety seconds, in pairs. Which features in this view would you use to set the map?
Then ask
Which of them will still be there next year — and which might not?
Linear features are best: rivers, walls, tracks, woodland edges. Then use the shape of the ground.
No labels. Name the features yourself.

slides.label: Confirming location
slides.notes: This is the assessed skill in miniature. Work through the diagram: a stream junction a hundred metres ahead, a shoulder on a steep slope, a wall you are in line with, a re-entrant passed fifteen minutes ago. No single one of those fixes you - together they do. Make the point that you should be collecting these as you walk, not scrambling for them once you are already lost.

slides.label: Section: Finding north
slides.notes: Second half. Frame it as the backup to the backup: no compass, no GPS, but you still need north. Three methods, each with its own conditions - one needs a clear night, two need sun. Say now that none of them is precise; they give you a direction good enough to set a map and walk out, not a bearing to navigate on.
slides.html:
Part Two
Finding north
without a compass
Good enough to set a map and walk out — not good enough to navigate on a bearing.

slides.label: Three methods
slides.notes: Overview slide - keep it to a minute. Three methods, and the conditions each one needs. Point out the obvious practical problem: the two sun methods are useless at night and the star method is useless under cloud, so knowing all three is the point. The shadow method is the slowest but needs no kit at all.
slides.html:
Finding north
Three methods
Method one
The Pole Star
Follow the pointers of the Plough.
NEEDS: a clear night sky
Method two
Using a watch
Bisect the angle between the hour hand and twelve.
NEEDS: sun, and an analogue watch
Method three
The shadow method
A stick, two stones, and fifteen minutes of patience.
NEEDS: sun bright enough to cast a shadow

slides.label: Pole Star
slides.notes: Get them to find the Plough on the diagram first, then the two pointer stars at the end of the pan. Extend that line about four times the gap between the pointers and you land on the Pole Star. That direction is north. Mention that the Plough rotates round the pole through the night and the seasons, so it may be upside down - the pointer trick still works whatever way up it is.
slides.html:
Finding north · method one
The Pole Star
In the northern hemisphere the Pole Star marks the direction of the north pole.
How to find it
Find the Great Bear (the Plough). Follow its two pointer stars, about four times their own spacing, and you arrive at the Pole Star.
The Plough turns through the night and the year — it may be upside down. The pointers still work.
Follow the pointers — roughly four times their own spacing (4d).

slides.label: Watch method
slides.notes: Demonstrate with a real watch if anyone has one. Hold it flat, hour hand at the sun, then bisect. The line you get points SOUTH - north is the opposite way, and cadets get this backwards constantly. The British Summer Time correction matters: April to October, bisect to the one o'clock position instead of twelve. Ask them what a digital watch owner does - draw the clock face on paper, or in the dirt.
slides.html:
Finding north · method two
Using a watch
1Hold the watch horizontally, hour hand pointing at the sun.
2On GMT, bisect the angle between the hour hand and twelve o’clock.
3On BST (April–October), bisect to the one o’clock position instead.
Get this right
That line points due SOUTH. North is the other way.
Hour hand to the sun; bisect to 12; that line runs south.

slides.label: Shadow method
slides.notes: Best done outside for real if the sun is out - set it running at the start of the lesson and come back to it. Stick upright, stone at the shadow tip, wait ten to fifteen minutes, second stone at the new tip. The line between the stones runs roughly west to east. Then from the stick through the midpoint of that line gives you north. Emphasise the wait: cadets always try to rush it and get a useless answer.
slides.html:
Finding north · method three
The shadow method
The sun must be bright enough to cast a shadow.
1Stick upright in the ground. Mark the tip of its shadow with a stone.
2Wait ten to fifteen minutes. Mark the new shadow tip with a second stone.
3The line between the two stones runs roughly west to east.
4Halve the distance between the stones. A line from the stick through that midpoint points north.
Do not rush the wait — a short gap gives a useless answer.
Stone 1 to stone 2 runs west–east; stick through halfway points north.

slides.label: ANIMATION Finding North
slides.notes: Run this after all three methods so cadets can compare them side by side. The animation shows the Plough rotating to the Pole Star, the watch bisection with the BST correction, and the shadow stones moving in real proportion. Stop after each method and ask which one they would actually use in the conditions outside right now.

slides.label: Recap
slides.notes: Close by checking the outcome, not the content. Ask three cadets in turn: set the map for me on this table; name four features you would use to confirm a position; find north with your watch. If they can do those, LO1 is met. Signpost LO2 - the three norths - and remind them the animation library is open at home.
slides.html:
Learning Outcome 1
Can you do these three things?
1
Set a map to the ground using a linear feature.
2
Name four features you would use to confirm a position.
3
Find north with a watch — and say which way is south.

prompts.text: What does ‘setting the map’ actually mean, and why do it before anything else?
Describe how you would find north without a compass. Which method would you trust most, and why?
What does a contour line tell you? How can you tell steep ground from gentle ground?
Name two features you could use to confirm your position on the ground.
